ref: 3.1.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput I, section 1
greek: Non enim per alios dispositionem salutis nostrae cognovimus, quam per eos per quos Evangelium pervenit ad nos: quod quidem tunc praeconaverunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in Scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum et columnam fidei nostrae futurum. Nec enim fas est dicere, quoniam ante praedicaverunt quam perfectam haberent agnitionem; sicut quidam audent dicere, gloriantes emendatores se esse Apostolorum. Postea enim quam surrexit Dominus noster a mortuis, et induti sunt supervenientis Spiritus sancti virtutem ex alto, de omnibus adimpleti sunt, et habuerunt perfectam agnitionem; exierunt in fines terrae, ea quae a Deo nobis bona sunt evangelizantes, et coelestem pacem hominibus annuntiantes, qui quidem et omnes pariter et singuli eorum habentes Evangelium Dei.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 2); "Non" is printed in small capitals, the djvu OCR reads "Now". Footnote 1 gives Arund. MS "praeconiaverunt".
english: We have learned from none others the plan of our salvation, than from those through whom the Gospel has come down to us, which they did at one time proclaim in public, and, at a later period, by the will of God, handed down to us in the Scriptures, to be the ground and pillar of our faith. For it is unlawful to assert that they preached before they possessed perfect knowledge, as some do even venture to say, boasting themselves as improvers of the apostles. For, after our Lord rose from the dead, [the apostles] were invested with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came down [upon them], were filled from all [His gifts], and had perfect knowledge: they departed to the ends of the earth, preaching the glad tidings of the good things [sent] from God to us, and proclaiming the peace of heaven to men, who indeed do all equally and individually possess the Gospel of God.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF page unknown; Harvey printed p. 2
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The apostles were given the Spirit's power from on high after the resurrection, and only then had perfect knowledge to preach.
limits: The Spirit is named as the power (virtus) that equips the apostles; the passage says nothing about the Spirit's divinity or personhood. Context is the Gospel's transmission, not the Trinity.

ref: 3.1.1 (ANF numbering); Eusebius HE 5.8.2-4 quoted in Harvey apparatus, Liber III Cap. I
greek: τοῦ Παύλου ἐν Ῥώμῃ εὐαγγελιζομένων, καὶ θεμελιούντων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν. Μετὰ δὲ τὴν τούτων ἔξοδον, Μάρκος ὁ μαθητὴς καὶ ἑρμηνευτὴς Πέτρου, καὶ αὐτὸς τὰ ὑπὸ Πέτρου κηρυσσόμενα ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν παραδέδωκε. Καὶ Λουκᾶς δὲ ὁ ἀκόλουθος Παύλου, τὸ ὑπ᾽ ἐκείνου κηρυσσόμενον εὐαγγέλιον ἐν βιβλίῳ κατέθετο. Ἔπειτα Ἰωάννης ὁ μαθητὴς τοῦ Κυρίου, ὁ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ ἀναπεσών, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐξέδωκε τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, ἐν Ἐφέσῳ τῆς Ἀσίας διατρίβων.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Greek apparatus, printed pp. 4-6 (PDF 15-17); read from the text layer and from the p. 6 page image. The sentence begins on p. 4 with a clause not transcribed here; the first words quoted are "τοῦ Παύλου".
english: Matthew also issued a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect, while Peter and Paul were preaching at Rome, and laying the foundations of the Church. After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, did also hand down to us in writing what had been preached by Peter. Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him. Afterwards, John, the disciple of the Lord, who also had leaned upon His breast, did himself publish a Gospel during his residence at Ephesus in Asia.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1) (English of the Latin, not of the Greek)
page: Harvey printed pp. 4-6 (apparatus); ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: Eusebius quotes, in Greek, Irenaeus on the order of the Gospels: Mark after the departure of Peter and Paul, Luke, then John at Ephesus.
limits: Greek is Eusebius's quotation, not Irenaeus's own Greek; the English is ANF's translation of the Latin, which has the same content. Not a Trinitarian passage: it is dating and transmission context only. The sentence on p. 4 is not transcribed.

ref: 3.1.2 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput I, section 1 (no separate section 2 marker seen in OCR)
greek: Et omnes isti unum Deum factorem coeli et terrae a lege et prophetis annuntiatum, et unum Christum filium Dei tradiderunt nobis: quibus si quis non assentit, spernit quidem participes Domini, spernit autem et ipsum Christum Dominum, spernit vero et Patrem, et est a semetipso damnatus, resistens et repugnans saluti suae: quod faciunt omnes haeretici.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 6).
english: These have all declared to us that there is one God, Creator of heaven and earth, announced by the law and the prophets; and one Christ the Son of God. If any one do not agree to these truths, he despises the companions of the Lord; nay more, he despises Christ Himself the Lord; yea, he despises the Father also, and stands self-condemned, resisting and opposing his own salvation, as is the case with all heretics.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 6; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The apostolic rule has one God, Creator, announced by law and prophets, and one Christ, the Son of God; denying either despises the Father too.
limits: The sentence names the Father, the Christ and the Son of God, but says nothing of the Spirit and nothing on the Son's co-equality; "unum Deum" is also used by unitarian readers.

ref: 3.4.2 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput IV, section 1
greek: Cui ordinationi assentiunt multae gentes barbarorum eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine charta vel atramento scriptam habentes per Spiritum in cordibus suis salutem, et veterem traditionem diligenter custodientes, in unum Deum credentes fabricatorem caeli et terrae, et omnium quae in eis sunt, per Christum Jesum Dei Filium.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 16).
english: To which course many nations of those barbarians who believe in Christ do assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink,
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 16; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: Barbarian nations who believe in Christ keep the tradition without writing, with salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, and believe in one God through the Son.
limits: The Spirit writes salvation in hearts (an inner work); the Spirit's divinity is not argued. The passage is about the rule of faith, not about the Trinity.

ref: 3.6.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VI, section 1
greek: 1. Neque igitur Dominus, neque Spiritus sanctus, neque Apostoli eum qui non esset Deus, definitive et absolute Deum nominassent aliquando, nisi esset vere Deus; neque Dominum appellassent aliquem ex sua persona, nisi qui dominatur omnium Deum Patrem, et Filium ejus qui dominium accepit a Patre suo omnis conditionis, quemadmodum habet illud: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede a dextris meis, quoadusque ponam inimicos tuos suppedaneum pedum tuorum. [...] Vere igitur cum Pater sit Dominus, et Filius vere sit Dominus, merito Spiritus sanctus Domini appellatione signavit eos.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page images (printed pp. 20-21). Harvey title of the chapter: "Ostensio quod in Scripturis nemo alius Deus nominatur, nec Dominus nuncupatur, nisi solus verus Deus Pater omnium et Verbum ejus."
english: Therefore neither would the Lord, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the apostles, have ever named as God, definitely and absolutely, him who was not God, unless he were truly God; nor would they have named any one in his own person Lord, except God the Father ruling over all, and His Son who has received dominion from His Father over all creation, as this passage has it: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make Your enemies Your footstool. Here the [Scripture] represents to us the Father addressing the Son; He who gave Him the inheritance of the heathen, and subjected to Him all His enemies. Since, therefore, the Father is truly Lord, and the Son truly Lord, the Holy Spirit has fitly designated them by the title of Lord.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed pp. 20-21; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The Lord, the Holy Spirit and the apostles never call "God" or "Lord" anyone who is not truly God; the Father and the Son are both Lord, and the Spirit names them with that title.
limits: The argument is from the scriptural use of divine names; it does not define a relation of being or use a technical term. The brief's quoted wording "the Father and the Son are rightly called God" does not occur in this sentence; the rightly-named phrase here is "Lord" (merito ... Domini appellatione).

ref: 3.6.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VI, section 1 (Psalm 44:7-8 and Psalm 82:1)
greek: Similiter habet illud: Sedes tua Deus in aeternum; virga directionis, virga regni tui. Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem, propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus. Utrosque enim Dei appellatione signavit Spiritus, et eum qui ungitur Filium, et eum qui ungit, id est Patrem. Et iterum: Deus stetit in synagoga Deorum, in medio autem deos discernit; de Patre, et Filio, et de his qui adoptionem perceperunt, dicit: hi autem sunt Ecclesia. Haec enim est synagoga Dei, quam Deus, hoc est Filius ipse per semetipsum collegit.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 21). Harvey note 3 on "Dominus... a Domino" cites early Fathers on the Son as the one who appeared to the patriarchs.
english: For the Spirit designates both [of them] by the name, of God — both Him who is anointed as Son, and Him who does anoint, that is, the Father. And again: God stood in the congregation of the gods, He judges among the gods. He [here] refers to the Father and the Son, and those who have received the adoption; but these are the Church. For she is the synagogue of God, which God— that is, the Son Himself — has gathered by Himself.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 21; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The Spirit designates both the anointed Son and the anointing Father by the name of God (Ps 44:7-8), and Psalm 82 speaks of the Father and the Son, with the adopted being the Church.
limits: The Son is called God by the Spirit's scriptural naming, not by an analysis of his being. The psalm's "gods" are read as Father, Son and the adopted (Church), which opponents will call forced. Harvey n.1 (Grabe) says Irenaeus uses the same Scripture texts as Justin, Dialogue with Trypho p. 277 (Justin not checked here).

ref: 3.6.2 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VI, section 2
greek: 2. Nemo igitur alius, quemadmodum praedixi, Deus nominatur, aut Dominus appellatur, nisi qui est omnium Deus et Dominus, qui et Moysi dixit: Ego sum, qui sum. Et sic dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos: et hujus Filius Jesus Christus Dominus noster, qui filios Dei facit credentes in nomen suum.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 22). Harvey note 2 (Grabe) remarks on Irenaeus applying Exodus 3:14 to the Father but Exodus 3:8 to the Son.
english: Wherefore, as I have already stated, no other is named as God, or is called Lord, except Him who is God and Lord of all, who also said to Moses, I am that I am. And thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He who is, has sent me unto you;
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 22; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: No one else is called God or Lord except the one God of all, who spoke to Moses as "I am who am"; that same name is given to the Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
limits: Read alone, "no other is called God" looks unitarian. Irenaeus's answer is that the Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, is the one who speaks to Moses in the name. Grabe (Harvey n.2) remarks with surprise that Irenaeus applies Ex 3:14 to the Father and Ex 3:8 to the Son, and explains it as mutual indwelling.

ref: 3.6.4 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VI, section 3
greek: 3. Et ego igitur invoco te Domine Deus Abraham, et Deus Isaac, et Deus Jacob et Israel, qui es Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Deus qui per multitudinem misericordiae tuae bene sensisti in nobis, ut te cognoscamus; qui fecisti coelum et terram, qui dominaris omnium, qui es solus et verus Deus, super quem alius Deus non est; per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum dominationem quoque dona Spiritus Sancti: da omni legenti hanc scripturam, cognoscere te quia solus Deus es, et confirmari in te, et absistere ab omni haeretica et quae est sine Deo et impia sententia.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 24).
english: Wherefore I do also call upon you, Lord God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob and Israel, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God who, through the abundance of Your mercy, has had a favour towards us
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 24; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: Irenaeus prays to the God of the patriarchs, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the only and true God, and asks that the Spirit's governing power be given through Jesus Christ.
limits: "qui es solus et verus Deus, super quem alius Deus non est" is addressed to the Father alone, and an Arian will read it as excluding the Son. The Son is present as the mediator of the gift ("per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum"). ANF renders "dominationem quoque dona" as "grant ... the governing power". The djvu OCR shows "Set" for "et"; the page image shows "et".

ref: 3.6.5 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VI, section 4
greek: 4. Et Apostolus autem Paulus, dicens: Si enim his qui non erant dii servistis, nunc cognoscentes Deum, imo cogniti a Deo, separavit eos qui non erant, ab eo qui est Deus. Et iterum de Antichristo dicens: Qui adversatur et extollit se, inquit, super omne quod dicitur deus, vel quod colitur, eos qui ab ignorantibus Deum dii dicuntur significat, id est idola. Etenim Pater omnium Deus dicitur, et est: et non super hunc extolletur Antichristus; sed super eos qui dicuntur quidem, non sunt autem dii.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 24).
english: He points out here those who are called gods, by such as know not God, that is, idols. For the Father of all is called God, and is so; and Antichrist shall be lifted up, not above Him, but above those which are indeed called gods, but are not.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 24; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: "The Father of all is called God, and is so": the idols are the false gods, and Antichrist will be exalted above them, not above the Father.
limits: The brief placed "the Father of all is called God" in 3.8.3; it is actually in 3.6.5. It is a unitarian-sounding claim about the Father, but the context is idols, not the Son. Irenaeus does not say the Father is alone God here.

ref: 3.8.3 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput VIII, section 3 (continues on the next page)
greek: 3. Quoniam enim sive Angeli, sive Archangeli, sive Throni, sive Dominationes, ab eo qui super omnes est Deus, et constituta sunt, et facta per Verbum ejus, Johannes quidem sic significavit. Cum enim dixisset de Verbo Dei, quoniam erat in Patre, adjecit: Omnia per eum facta sunt, et sine eo factum est nihil. [...] ita ut is quidem qui omnia fecerit, cum Verbo suo juste dicatur Deus et Dominus solus; quae autem facta sunt, non jam ejusdem vocabuli participabilia esse, neque juste id vocabulum sumere debere, quod est Creatoris.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page images (printed pp. 29-30). Harvey note 4 (Grabe) says: "Ne haec verba male accipias, lege egregiam plane fidei Nicaenae defensionem, G. Bulli p. 133."
english: For that all things, whether Angels, or Archangels, or Thrones, or Dominions, were both established and created by Him who is God over all, through His Word, John has thus pointed out. For when he had spoken of the Word of God as having been in the Father, he added, All things were made by Him, and without Him was not anything made. John 1:3 David also, when he had enumerated [His] praises, subjoins by name all things whatsoever I have mentioned, both the heavens and all the powers therein: For He commanded, and they were created; He spoke, and they were made. Whom, therefore, did He command? The Word, no doubt, by whom, he says, the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth. But that He did Himself make all things freely, and as He pleased, again David says, But our God is in the heavens above, and in the earth; He has made all things whatsoever He pleased. But the things established are distinct from Him who has established them, and what have been made from Him who has made them. For He is Himself uncreated, both without beginning and end, and lacking nothing. He is Himself sufficient for Himself; and still further, He grants to all others this very thing, existence; but the things which have been made by Him have received a beginning. But whatever things had a beginning, and are liable to dissolution, and are subject to and stand in need of Him who made them, must necessarily in all respects have a different term [applied to them], even by those who have but a moderate capacity for discerning such things; so that He indeed who made all things can alone, together with His Word, properly be termed God and Lord: but the things which have been made cannot have this term applied to them, neither should they justly assume that appellation which belongs to the Creator.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed pp. 29-30; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: All things were made through the Word by the God over all; but the Creator alone, "together with His Word", is properly called God and Lord.
limits: Read alone, "Deus et Dominus solus" is the strongest unitarian line in the chapter; the words "cum Verbo suo" are the answer, and Harvey's note sends the reader to Bull. The English of the ANF phrase is "together with His Word", the Latin "cum Verbo suo". The brief's "Father of all" is not in this section (see I3-09).

ref: 3.9.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput IX, section 1
greek: 1. Ostenso hoc igitur hic plane, et adhuc ostendetur manifestius, neminem alterum Dominum vel Deum, neque prophetas, neque Apostolos, neque Dominum Christum confessum esse ex sua persona, sed praecipue Deum et Dominum: prophetis quidem et Apostolis Patrem et Filium confitentibus; alterum autem neminem, neque Deum nominantibus, neque Dominum confitentibus: et ipso Domino Patrem tantum Deum et Dominum eum, qui solus est Deus et dominator omnium, tradente discipulis;
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 30). Harvey prints "Ostenso" as "Osrenso" in the OCR.
english: This, therefore, having been clearly demonstrated here (and it shall yet be so still more clearly), that neither the prophets, nor the apostles, nor the Lord Christ in His own person, did acknowledge any other Lord or God, but the God and Lord supreme: the prophets and the apostles confessing the Father and the Son; but naming no other as God, and confessing no other as Lord: and the Lord Himself handing down to His disciples, that He, the Father, is the only God and Lord, who alone is God and ruler of all;
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 30; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: No prophet, apostle or Christ confessed any other God or Lord than the supreme one; the prophets and apostles confessed the Father and the Son, and the Lord taught that the Father alone is God and Lord and ruler of all.
limits: This is the strongest passage for an Arian or unitarian reader: "Patrem tantum Deum et Dominum... qui solus est Deus". The contrast is with "any other" God (the Demiurge, Marcion), and the sentence itself says the prophets and apostles confessed the Father AND the Son. No answer in the text about the Spirit. Defenders (Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae) and critics must still be checked; not read here.

ref: 3.9.1 (ANF numbering, second half); Harvey Liber III, Caput IX, section 2
greek: 2. Unus igitur et idem Deus est, Pater Domini nostri, qui et praecursorem per prophetas missurum se promisit: et salutare suum, id est Verbum suum, visibile effecit omni fieri carni, incarnatum et ipsum, ut in omnibus manifestus fieret Rex eorum. [...] Unus igitur et idem Deus, qui a prophetis praedicatus est, et ab evangelio annuntiatus, et hujus Filius qui ex fructu ventris David, id est ex David Virgine, et Emmanuel:
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 31).
english: There is therefore one and the same God, the Father of our Lord, who also promised, through the prophets, that He would send His forerunner; and His salvation
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 31; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: There is one and the same God, the Father of our Lord; his salvation, that is his Word, was made visible to all flesh by becoming incarnate, and the Son is the son of David and Emmanuel.
limits: The sentence identifies the Word with God's salvation and the Son with Emmanuel. It does not say the Word is God in so many words; "one and the same God" is the phrase on which opponents also rely.

ref: 3.9.3 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput X (Harvey does not number the section in the OCR)
greek: Adhuc ait in baptismate Matthaeus: Aperti sunt [ei] coeli, et vidit Spiritum Dei quasi columbam venientem super eum. Et ecce vox de coelo, dicens: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui. Non enim Christus tunc descendit in Jesum; neque alius quidem Christus, alius vero Jesus: sed Verbum Dei, qui est Salvator omnium, et dominator coeli et terrae, qui est Jesus, quemadmodum ante ostendimus, qui et assumsit carnem, et unctus est a Patre Spiritu, Jesus Christus factus est;
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 32). "[ei]" is bracketed in the print, with footnote 2 (Clerm. and Ar. MSS omit it).
english: And then, [speaking of His] baptism, Matthew says, The heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God, as a dove, coming upon Him: and lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Matthew 3:16 For Christ did not at that time descend upon Jesus, neither was Christ one and Jesus another: but the Word of God— who is the Saviour of all, and the ruler of heaven and earth, who is Jesus, as I have already pointed out, who did also take upon Him flesh, and was anointed by the Spirit from the Father — was made Jesus Christ
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 32; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: At the baptism the Spirit of God descended on Jesus; the Word of God, who became Jesus Christ, was anointed "by the Spirit from the Father".
limits: The Spirit is an anointing given by the Father to the Word-made-flesh. "a Patre Spiritu" is ambiguous (Spirit from the Father, or the Father by the Spirit); no statement of the Spirit's personhood or divinity.

ref: 3.11.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XI, section 7
greek: 7. Hanc fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaitae, [...] ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: [...] et initium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quae est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta,
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 40). Harvey n.1: "Sic quidem unus et idem Deus"; the Clerm. MS. reads "sic idem et unus Deus".
english: John, the disciple of the Lord, preaches this faith, and seeks, by the proclamation of the Gospel, to remove that error which by Cerinthus had been disseminated among men, and a long time previously by those termed Nicolaitans, who are an offset of that knowledge falsely so called, that he might confound them, and persuade them that there is but one God, who made all things by His Word
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 40; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: John's Gospel is directed against the teaching that the Creator was another than the Father of the Lord: there is one God, who made all things by His Word; the Logos is the true son of the Only-begotten.
limits: "made all things by His Word" is instrumental language, which subordinationists also use. The Logos is called "verum filium unigeniti" in the Gnostic system Irenaeus is refuting, so the Logos-as-Son point is the opponents' term, not his own.

ref: 3.11.3 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XI, section 8
greek: 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Etenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hunc mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; [...] Secundum autem nullam sententiam haereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 42). Harvey n.1 on p. 46 (Cerinthians, Basilidians) concerns the preceding section.
english: But, according to these men, neither was the Word made flesh, nor Christ, nor the Saviour (Soter), who was produced from [the joint contributions of] all [the Æons]. For they will have it, that the Word and Christ never came into this world; that the Saviour, too, never became incarnate, nor suffered, but that He descended like a dove upon the dispensational Jesus; and that, as soon as He had declared the unknown Father, He did again ascend into the Pleroma. Some, however, make the assertion, that this dispensational Jesus did become incarnate, and suffered, whom they represent as having passed through Mary just as water through a tube; but others allege him to be the Son of the Demiurge, upon whom the dispensational Jesus descended; while others, again, say that Jesus was born from Joseph and Mary, and that the Christ from above descended upon him, being without flesh, and impassible. But according to the opinion of no one of the heretics was the Word of God made flesh. For if anyone carefully examines the systems of them all, he will find that the Word of God is brought in
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 42; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The heretics deny that the Word of God became flesh; Irenaeus says no heretic's system allows the Word of God to be incarnate.
limits: Irenaeus's statement (John 1:14 quoted at the head of the page) is about the incarnation of the Word, not about the Word's eternal relation to the Father. The Latin quote of John 1:14 is printed in the same page.

ref: 3.11.8 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XI, section 11
greek: 11. Neque autem plura numero quam haec sunt, neque rursus pauciora capit esse Evangelia. Quoniam enim quatuor regiones mundi sunt in quo sumus, et quatuor principales spiritus, et deseminata est Ecclesia super omnem terram, columna autem et firmamentum Ecclesiae est Evangelium, et spiritus vitae; consequens est, quatuor habere eam columnas, undique flantes incorruptibilitatem, et vivificantes homines. Ex quibus manifestum est, quoniam qui est omnium artifex Verbum, qui sedet super Cherubim, et continet omnia, declaratus hominibus, dedit nobis quadriforme Evangelium, quod uno spiritu continetur.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page images (printed pp. 46-47).
english: It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are. For, since there are four zones of the world in which we live, and four principal winds, while the Church is scattered throughout all the world, and the pillar and ground 1 Timothy 3:15 of the Church is the Gospel and the spirit of life; it is fitting that she should have four pillars, breathing out immortality on every side, and vivifying men afresh. From which fact, it is evident that the Word, the Artificer of all, He that sits upon the cherubim, and contains all things, He who was manifested to men, has given us the Gospel under four aspects, but bound together by one Spirit.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed pp. 46-47; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: There are four Gospels because there are four regions and four winds, and the Word, the artificer of all, gave the Gospel in four forms, held together by one Spirit.
limits: The brief said this section mentions "the Spirit". Here "spiritus" in the four-winds argument means winds, and "spiritus vitae" is the Gospel, so this is not a Holy Spirit passage. "quod uno spiritu continetur" is ambiguous (the Holy Spirit or the Spirit of life) and Harvey gives no decision.

ref: 3.11.8 (ANF numbering); Anastasius, Quaestiones et responsiones 144, printed by Harvey as a fragment in note 4 to Liber III, Caput XI, section 11
greek: Ἐπειδὴ καὶ τέσσαρα κλίματα τοῦ κόσμου ἐν ᾧ ἐσμὲν εἰσὶ, καὶ τέσσαρα καθολικὰ πνεύματα, κατέσπαρται δὲ ἡ ἐκκλησία ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς γῆς, στύλος δὲ καὶ στήριγμα ἐκκλησίας τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, καὶ πνεῦμα ζωῆς· εἰκότως τέσσαρας ἔχειν αὐτὴν στύλους, πανταχόθεν πνέοντας τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν, καὶ ἀναζωπυροῦντας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους. Ἐξ ὧν φανερὸν, ὅτι ὁ τῶν ἁπάντων τεχνίτης Λόγος, ὁ καθήμενος ἐπὶ τῶν Χερουβὶμ καὶ συνέχων τὰ πάντα, φανερωθεὶς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν τετράμορφον τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, ἑνὶ δὲ πνεύματι συνεχόμενον.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan, note 4 (Greek type, printed p. 47). Read from page image (PDF page 58). Harvey says it is Irenaeus's passage "tacito licet Irenaei nomine, paucisque mutatis" given as the answer to Anastasius Q. 144 (Florentine MS of Anastasius, transcribed by Morus).
english: From which fact, it is evident that the Word, the Artificer of all, He that sits upon the cherubim, and contains all things, He who was manifested to men, has given us the Gospel under four aspects, but bound together by one Spirit.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1) (English of the Latin; the Greek is not translated by ANF)
page: Harvey printed p. 47, note 4
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The Greek repeats the Latin argument for four Gospels, with the Word as artificer of all, and the Gospel "held together by one Spirit".
limits: This is not Irenaeus's own Greek text: Harvey says it is taken from Anastasius with the name of Irenaeus omitted and a few words changed. Use it only as a witness to the wording, not as an autograph. The Spirit is not defined.

ref: 3.12.1 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XII, section 1
greek: 1. Petrus igitur Apostolus post resurrectionem Domini, et assumtionem in coelos, volens adimplere duodecim Apostolorum numerum, et allegere pro Juda alterum, qui electus esset a Deo, his qui aderant, dixit: Viri fratres, oportebat impleri Scripturam hanc, quam [OCR garbled] Spiritus sanctus ore David de Juda, qui factus est dux his qui apprehenderunt Jesum, [...] Rursus cum Spiritus sanctus descendisset in discipulos, uti omnes prophetarent, et loquerentur linguis, et quidam irriderent eos, quasi a musto ebrios; [...] Erit in novissimis diebus, dicit Dominus, effundam de Spiritu meo in omnem carnem, et prophetabunt. Deus igitur, qui per prophetam promisit missurum se Spiritum suum in humanum genus, ipse et misit [ei] et ipse Deus a Petro annuntiatur, suam promissionem adimplesse.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from the text layer and OCR (printed pp. 52-53, PDF 63-64); not checked against the page image.
english: The God, therefore, who did promise by the prophet, that He would send His Spirit upon the whole human race, was He who did send
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed pp. 52-53; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: Peter says the Holy Spirit spoke through David, and that the Spirit, poured out at Pentecost, is the promised gift that God, who promised it, sent.
limits: The Spirit appears as a promised gift sent by God; the text does not discuss the Spirit's personhood or divinity. The OCR garbles one word ("quam ...") in the Latin, so the exact wording needs a page-image check before any citation.

ref: 3.12.14 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XII, section 17
greek: Placuit enim sancto Spiritui, et nobis, nullum amplius vobis pondus imponere, quam haec quae sunt necessaria, ut abstineatis ab idolothytis, et sanguine, et fornicatione: et quaecunque non vultis fieri vobis, aliis ne faciatis: a quibus custodientes vos ipsos, bene agetis, ambulantes in Spiritu sancto.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from the OCR text (printed p. 70, PDF 81); not checked against the page image. The OCR reads "Placwit" and "Sambulantes".
english: For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; that you abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from fornication; and whatsoever you do not wish to be done to you, do not to others: from which preserving yourselves, you shall do well, walking in the Holy Spirit
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 70; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The Acts 15 decree was "pleasing to the Holy Spirit and to us", and the believers walk in the Holy Spirit.
limits: The Spirit is named beside the apostles as a joint agent of a decision, which is a Lukan quotation; Irenaeus does not draw doctrinal conclusions. Not a statement of the Spirit's divinity.

ref: 3.13.2 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XIII, section 2
greek: 2. Et Dominus autem Philippo volenti Patrem videre, respondit: Tanto tempore vobiscum sum, et me non cognovisti, Philippe? qui videt me, videt et Patrem. Quomodo tu dicis, Ostende nobis Patrem? Ego enim in Patre, et Pater in me, et a modo cognovistis eum, et vidistis. [...] Sicut ergo Paulus Apostolus non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum et Deum Patrem; Filio quidem adducente eos ad Patrem, Patre vero revelante eis Filium.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from page image (printed p. 73). Harvey n.2: "Christum" restored by Grabe from the Arundel MS., but cancelled again by Massuet.
english: And again, the Lord replied to Philip, who wished to behold the Father, Have I been so long a time with you, and yet you have not known Me, Philip? He that sees Me, sees also the Father; and how do you say then, Show us the Father? For I am in the Father, and the Father in Me; and henceforth you know Him, and have seen Him.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 73; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: Quoting John 14:9-10 on Philip, Irenaeus says the Son and the Father are mutually in each other, so the one who sees the Son sees the Father.
limits: This is a Johannine argument about revelation and mutual indwelling, not an ontological analysis. The Latin "Christum" in "per Jesum Christum et Deum Patrem" was restored by Grabe and cancelled by Massuet (Harvey n.2). Unitarian readers take "Filio adducente, Patre revelante" as a relation of order.

ref: 3.14.2 (ANF numbering); Harvey Liber III, Caput XIV, section 2 (approximate)
greek: Attendite igitur et vobis, et omni gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus proposuit episcopos, regere ecclesiam Domini, quam sibi constituit per sanguinem suum.
greek_edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan. Read from the OCR text (printed p. 76, PDF 87); not checked against the page image. OCR garbles "Attendite" area.
english: Take heed, therefore, both to yourselves, and to all the flock over which the Holy Ghost has placed you as bishops, to rule the Church of the Lord, which He has acquired for Himself through His own blood
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: Harvey printed p. 76; ANF page unknown
edition: Harvey, Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1857); Latin printed with Harvey apparatus; printed pages as in the scan | English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; printed page not shown
what_it_says: The Holy Spirit placed the elders as bishops over the Church, which the Lord acquired by his own blood.
limits: The Spirit is the agent of the Church's appointments; there is no doctrine of the Spirit's divinity here. Included only as a Spirit mention from ch. 14, the last of the brief's range.
